system: Yoga and meditation practices matched to the chart - a modern Jyotish-Ayurveda layer, not part of the Parashari knowledge base
sources: Svatmarama, Hatha Yoga Pradipika (15th c.): Trataka 2.31-32, Kapalabhati 2.35, Nadi Shodhana 2.7-10, Ujjayi 2.51-53, Sheetali 2.57-58, Bhastrika 2.59-67, Bhramari 2.68, Kumbhaka 2.44-48, Maha Bandha 3.19-24, Uddiyana 3.55-60, Mula 3.61-69, Jalandhara 3.70-73
Gheranda Samhita (Trataka 1.53-54, Kapalabhati 1.55-56); Patanjali, Yoga Sutras (1.34, 2.1, 2.44)
Swami Satyananda Saraswati (Bihar School of Yoga): Yoga Nidra; Kundalini Tantra (Ajapa japa, chakra awareness as preparation); Chandra Bhedana
Planet-to-practice and Moon-element matching follow the modern Jyotish-Ayurveda approach (for example David Frawley, Ayurvedic Astrology, 2005); it is not found in BPHS
Age bands after Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana 8.122 (stages of life), with a separate band under 18
Contraindications from standard yoga-therapy guidance (forceful breathing: pregnancy, high blood pressure, heart disease, hernia, epilepsy, vertigo; breath retention as for locks)
safety: These are traditional practices, not medical treatment. If you have a health condition, are pregnant, or take regular medication, check with your doctor first. Advanced practices are shown with full instructions because they are classical, but they should be learned from a qualified teacher in person.

cautions.general: Stop if you feel dizzy, breathless, anxious or unwell, and breathe normally. Never force the breath or hold it with strain.
cautions.empty_stomach: Practise on an empty stomach (two to three hours after a meal).
cautions.forceful_breath: Not in pregnancy, or with high blood pressure, heart disease, a hernia, recent abdominal surgery, epilepsy, vertigo or a stomach ulcer. Avoid it during the heaviest days of the period.
cautions.eyes: Not with epilepsy or a seizure history, glaucoma or a recent eye operation. Blink and close the eyes whenever they sting; do not force the gaze.
cautions.retention: Breath holding and the locks are not for pregnancy, high or very low blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, epilepsy, a hernia or recent surgery, or a history of panic attacks, psychosis or bipolar disorder.
cautions.teacher: Learn this from a qualified teacher in person; the classical texts themselves say these methods must be learned under guidance.
cautions.warning_signs: Stop at once and get help from a teacher or doctor if you notice headaches, a racing heart, sleeplessness, strong anxiety or mood swings, involuntary shaking, or heat or electric-like sensations that do not settle.
cautions.joints: Move within your comfortable range; skip or soften any pose that hurts the back, knees or wrists.
cautions.cold: Skip in cold weather or with a cold, asthma or low blood pressure (it cools the body).

practices.name: Surya Namaskar (Sun salutation)
practices.source: A traditional flowing sequence, standardised in the 20th century
practices.why: Twelve linked postures done facing the rising Sun build warmth, stamina and a sense of purpose.
steps: Stand facing east at sunrise, feet together, palms joined at the chest.
Move through the twelve postures slowly, breathing in as you open and lift, out as you fold and bend.
Start with three rounds; add one a week, up to twelve.
Finish lying flat for a minute, breathing normally.

practices.name: Sunrise mantra (Gayatri or the Sun's seed mantra)
practices.source: Vedic sunrise worship (sandhya); seed mantra from the app's mantra table
practices.why: A short, regular mantra at sunrise steadies confidence and links the day to a fixed rhythm.
steps: Sit facing east soon after sunrise, back straight.
Offer a little water towards the Sun if you wish.
Repeat the Gayatri or the Sun's seed mantra 108 times on a mala, silently or softly.

practices.name: Trataka (candle-flame gazing)
practices.why: Steady gazing at one small point gathers a scattered mind into one place; the texts say it removes lethargy.
steps: Sit in a dark, draught-free room with a candle at arm's length, the flame level with your eyes.
Gaze softly at the tip of the wick without straining, blinking as little as is comfortable.
When the eyes water or tire, close them and watch the after-image at the brow until it fades.
Start with one minute of gazing; build up slowly over weeks to about ten.

practices.name: Chandra Bhedana (left-nostril breathing)
practices.source: Bihar School of Yoga (the cooling counterpart of Surya Bhedana, Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.48-50)
practices.why: Breathing in through the left nostril is used to cool and calm, and to settle a restless or heated mind.
steps: Sit comfortably. Close the right nostril with the right thumb.
Breathe in slowly through the left nostril.
Close the left nostril with the ring finger and breathe out through the right.
Repeat for 9 to 27 rounds, breathing smoothly with no holding.

practices.name: Sheetali (cooling breath)
practices.why: Breathing in over a curled tongue cools the body and calms anger and impatience.
steps: Sit straight. Curl the tongue into a tube (or breathe through closed teeth if you cannot).
Breathe in slowly through the tongue, then close the mouth and breathe out through the nose.
Repeat 9 to 15 times.

practices.name: Yoga Nidra (guided deep relaxation)
practices.source: Swami Satyananda Saraswati, Yoga Nidra (Bihar School of Yoga)
practices.why: Lying still while moving awareness through the body brings deep rest, eases worry and helps sleep.
steps: Lie on your back with a light cover; set a simple, positive intention.
Move your attention slowly through each part of the body, right side then left.
Notice the breath, then sensations of heaviness and lightness.
Repeat your intention, then return slowly; or follow a recorded Yoga Nidra.

practices.name: Nadi Shodhana (alternate-nostril breathing)
practices.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.7-10 (practised here without breath holding)
practices.why: Balances the two sides of the breath; used to calm nerves, clear thinking and steady restlessness.
steps: Sit straight. Close the right nostril and breathe in through the left.
Close the left, open the right and breathe out; breathe in through the right.
Close the right, open the left and breathe out. That is one round.
Do 9 to 15 rounds with an even count (for example 4 in, 4 out), with no holding.

practices.name: Mantra japa for the planet
practices.source: Traditional japa; seed mantras from the app's mantra table
practices.why: Repeating a planet's mantra with attention is the classical way to work with that planet's energy.
steps: Sit quietly on the planet's day, ideally at its traditional time.
Repeat the planet's seed mantra (shown with the planet above) 108 times on a mala.
Keep the attention on the sound; when the mind wanders, return gently.

practices.name: Svadhyaya (reflective study)
practices.why: Slow reading of a wisdom text, followed by quiet reflection, nourishes Jupiter's side of you: meaning and judgement.
steps: Choose a wisdom text you respect (the Gita, the Upanishads, or another).
Read one short passage slowly, twice.
Sit with eyes closed for a few minutes and let one line sink in; write a sentence about it if you like.

practices.name: Gratitude and teacher meditation
practices.why: Bringing to mind the teachers and blessings in your life opens the heart and strengthens trust.
steps: Sit quietly and breathe slowly for a minute.
Picture a teacher, elder or guide who helped you; silently thank them.
Name three things you are grateful for today, and rest in that feeling.

practices.name: Bhramari (humming-bee breath)
practices.why: A soft hum on the out-breath quietens the mind and is used to ease tension and worry.
steps: Sit straight, close the eyes; lightly close the ears with the index fingers if comfortable.
Breathe in through the nose, then hum like a bee as you breathe out, slowly and evenly.
Repeat 7 to 11 times, then sit and listen to the silence.

practices.name: Devotional singing and heart meditation
practices.why: Singing or listening to devotional music and resting attention at the heart softens and uplifts the feelings.
steps: Sing or listen to a devotional song or chant you love, for a few minutes.
Then sit quietly with attention at the centre of the chest.
Let a feeling of warmth or kindness grow there, and wish well to someone you love.

practices.name: Silent sitting with breath awareness
practices.why: Simply watching the natural breath builds patience, steadiness and the ability to stay with difficulty.
steps: Sit upright and still, eyes closed.
Feel the breath at the nostrils without changing it.
When thoughts pull you away, notice it and return to the breath, without judging yourself.
Keep the same time each day; regularity matters more than length.

practices.name: Walking meditation
practices.why: Slow, attentive walking grounds a busy or anxious mind in the body and the present moment.
steps: Walk slowly on a quiet path or back and forth in a room.
Feel each foot lift, move and touch the ground.
When the mind drifts, come back to the feet.

practices.name: Seva (selfless service)
practices.why: Regular, quiet help to others, especially the elderly, workers or those in need, is the traditional way to work with Saturn.
steps: Choose one simple, regular act of service: helping an elder, volunteering, feeding the hungry.
Do it without expecting thanks or reward.
Saturdays are traditional, but steadiness matters more than the day.

practices.name: Ujjayi (ocean breath)
practices.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.51-53 (practised here without breath holding)
practices.why: A slow breath with a soft sound in the throat lengthens the breath and settles the nerves.
steps: Sit straight. Slightly narrow the back of the throat so the breath makes a soft whisper.
Breathe in and out through the nose, slowly and evenly, listening to the sound.
Continue for 5 to 10 minutes, with no holding.

practices.name: Steady strength-building asana
practices.why: Standing and balancing postures held with steady breath channel Mars's drive into strength instead of irritation.
steps: Warm up for a few minutes.
Hold standing postures (warrior, triangle, tree) for five slow breaths each side.
Finish with a forward bend and two minutes lying still; follow with a few rounds of Sheetali if you feel heated.

practices.name: Kapalabhati (skull-shining breath)
practices.why: Short, active out-breaths with passive in-breaths energise a dull or sluggish state; it is a cleansing practice, used briefly.
steps: Sit straight on an empty stomach.
Breathe out sharply through the nose by pulling the belly in; let the in-breath happen by itself.
Start with one round of 20 breaths at a comfortable pace, then breathe normally for a minute.
Build up slowly to three rounds; never continue through dizziness.

practices.name: Bhastrika (bellows breath)
practices.why: Forceful in- and out-breaths build heat and energy; the texts call it powerful and it needs care.
steps: Learn it with a teacher first.
Sit straight on an empty stomach; breathe in and out forcefully and equally through the nose, about 10 times.
Then take one slow, deep breath and breathe normally until fully settled before any next round.
Keep to one to three short rounds.

practices.name: So-Ham breath awareness (Ajapa japa)
practices.source: Swami Satyananda Saraswati, Kundalini Tantra; Hamsa Upanishad
practices.why: Hearing 'So' on the in-breath and 'Ham' on the out-breath is the gentle doorway to Kundalini work: steady, inward and safe.
steps: Sit straight, eyes closed, breathing naturally.
Silently hear 'So' as you breathe in and 'Ham' as you breathe out.
Let the breath slow by itself; if you like, feel it rise from the navel to the throat and fall again.

practices.name: Chakra awareness (gentle Kundalini preparation)
practices.source: Swami Satyananda Saraswati, Kundalini Tantra (preparatory stage)
practices.why: Resting attention briefly at each of the seven centres, from the base of the spine to the crown, builds the sensitivity the deeper practices need.
steps: Sit straight and breathe naturally.
Move your attention slowly up the spine: base, lower belly, navel, heart, throat, eyebrow centre, crown.
Stay three to five breaths at each point, simply noticing; do not try to force any sensation.
Come back down to the heart and end there.

practices.name: Mula Bandha (root lock)
practices.why: A gentle lift of the pelvic floor; in Hatha yoga it is the first of the three locks used to direct energy upwards.
steps: Learn it with a teacher first.
Sit straight. Gently draw up the muscles at the base of the trunk, as if stopping the flow of urine, while breathing normally.
Hold for five breaths without straining, then release fully. Repeat 5 times.

practices.name: Uddiyana Bandha (abdominal lock)
practices.why: Drawing the belly in and up after a full out-breath; the texts praise it highly and it must be learned carefully.
steps: Learn it with a teacher first, and only on a completely empty stomach.
Stand with hands on knees. Breathe out fully, then, without breathing in, draw the belly in and up under the ribs.
Hold only as long as is comfortable (a few seconds at first), release the belly, then breathe in slowly.
Do 3 rounds at most, breathing normally between them.

practices.name: Jalandhara Bandha (chin lock)
practices.why: Lowering the chin to the chest during a held breath; the texts use it to keep the held breath safe.
steps: Learn it with a teacher first.
Sit straight, breathe in, and gently lower the chin towards the chest while lengthening the back of the neck.
Hold only a few comfortable seconds, lift the head, then breathe out slowly.
Never hold the breath to the point of strain.

practices.name: Kumbhaka (gentle breath retention)
practices.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.44-48; ratios after Bihar School practice
practices.why: Pausing the breath after the in-breath deepens concentration; the texts make it the heart of pranayama and warn against force.
steps: Learn it with a teacher first, after months of comfortable Nadi Shodhana.
During Nadi Shodhana, after breathing in, pause for an equal count (for example 4 in, 4 hold, 4 out).
Increase the count only when it is completely easy, over weeks; the out-breath must never be rushed.
Use Jalandhara Bandha during any hold longer than a few seconds.

practices.name: Maha Bandha (the three locks together)
practices.why: The root, abdominal and chin locks held together on an out-breath; the texts call it the great lock and the culmination of the bandhas.
steps: Only after each lock is easy on its own, and only with a teacher.
Breathe out fully, then apply Jalandhara, Uddiyana and Mula Bandha in that order.
Hold only a few comfortable seconds, release in reverse order (Mula, Uddiyana, Jalandhara), then breathe in slowly.
Do 3 rounds at most, with normal breathing between them.

Moon.theme: a calm mind, rest and emotional balance

Mars.theme: steady energy, courage and patience instead of anger

Mercury.theme: clear thinking, calm nerves and careful speech

Jupiter.theme: wisdom, trust, gratitude and good judgement

Venus.theme: warmth, harmony and a sense of beauty

Saturn.theme: patience, discipline and steadiness under pressure

Rahu.theme: grounding, clarity and calm amid restlessness

Ketu.theme: focus, inner quiet and letting go

fire.why: Your Moon is in a fire sign, so a focused, one-pointed practice suits the mind; cool it afterwards if you feel heated.

earth.why: Your Moon is in an earth sign, so a practice through the body and the senses settles the mind most easily.

air.why: Your Moon is in an air sign, so a balancing breath practice steadies a quick, busy mind.

water.why: Your Moon is in a water sign, so sound, mantra and feeling-based practice suit the mind best.

ages.label: Under 18
ages.advice: Gentle practices only. Strong breathing, breath holding and the Kundalini locks are left out until adulthood.

ages.label: 18-29 (youth, the Kapha stage of life)
ages.advice: Energy is high: active practices suit you, balanced with stillness. A good time to build a steady daily habit.

ages.label: 30-59 (middle age, the Pitta stage of life)
ages.advice: Work and family load are highest: short, regular, calming practices fit best. Cool the system rather than heat it.

ages.label: 60 and over (the Vata stage of life)
ages.advice: Gentle, grounding and restful practices suit this stage. Strong breathing and new breath-holding or lock practices are not advised unless you already practise them with a teacher and your doctor agrees.

levels.advanced: Advanced - adults, learned with a teacher
